title: Dhotaka's question (Sn 5)
hook: read it: I can't free you; know the teaching and cross yourself
tomorrow: if you have to cross alone, what do you hold onto?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mettagu's question, and a week gathered under one line: where it comes from. Suffering grows from what's taken up and held. Then a harder question: can someone else just set you free?
screen: `WHERE IT COMES FROM.` → `CAN SOMEONE ELSE SET YOU FREE?`

segments.voice: Midnight before the exam, and the message to the friend who gets it: please, just send me your answers. Or the call to a parent: just tell me what to do. Now the same moment, long ago. A young man named Dhotaka has come a long way with other students to question the Buddha. He's already asked once to hear the teaching. Now he bows. I see you, he says, a sage who owns nothing, walking the world. I bow to you. Free me from my doubts. And the Buddha says: I can't.
screen: `JUST SEND ME YOUR ANSWERS.` → `DHOTAKA BOWS.` → `FREE ME FROM MY DOUBTS.` → `I CAN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the rest of that line, in Dhotaka's question. I am not able to free anyone in the world who has doubts. But when you know the best teaching, you will cross this flood yourself. It lands hard at first. The student is on his knees, and the teacher says no. But listen to what's inside the no. The Buddha doesn't send him away. Earlier in the same exchange he's already told him: be ardent, wise and mindful, listen, and train yourself toward peace. After the no, he keeps teaching. He offers to describe a peace that isn't hearsay, one you can see for yourself here and now, and says: whatever you know, above, below, across, in the middle, see it as a tie to the world, and don't build craving on it. So the no isn't a closed door. It's a map, and a refusal to carry him. Doubt, in this story, isn't something a teacher can lift off you like a coat. It clears when you walk. That's the strange respect in the answer: the Buddha treats Dhotaka as someone able to cross. The teaching is given; the crossing is his. And the far shore in these poems is the image for that whole path. Nobody gets ferried. Each one crosses.
screen: `I CANNOT FREE ANYONE.` · `KNOW THE TEACHING, CROSS THE FLOOD.` · `THE NO IS A MAP.` · `DOUBT CLEARS WHEN YOU WALK.` · then, large: `CROSS YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand up and take a few slow steps, as slow as you can manage. Feel each foot lift, move and land, and notice that no one else can take this step for you. Then sit again and rest, feeling the floor under your feet until the bell.
Dhotaka's question: a student bows and asks to be freed from doubt. The Buddha says he can't free anyone, but whoever knows the teaching crosses the flood themselves.
For the riverbank in front of you: cross yourself, with the map in hand. Day sixteen seventy-four, walked.

screen: `DAY 1674 COUNTS.` → `THE WAY TO THE FAR SHORE · 3 OF 8.` → `TOMORROW: CROSSING ALONE, WHAT DO YOU HOLD?`

howItsDone: Theravada teachers often cite Dhotaka's question alongside the saying that the Buddhas only point the way: the teaching is offered, and each person practices it themselves.

fork.setup: your little brother is stuck on a hard puzzle and begs you to just solve it. what would Dhotaka's answer have you do?
options: show him how to look at it, then let him find the last move himself.
solve it for him; helping means taking the hard part away.
walk off and tell him he's on his own, since nobody can help.
fork.reveal: the Buddha said no to carrying Dhotaka, and then kept teaching. the way is shown; the crossing is the student's own.

original.note: Pali: flood. The flood each student asks how to cross.

chat.meaning: The Buddha told Dhotaka he couldn't free him, then kept teaching. A guide shows the way; the crossing belongs to the one who walks.

Dhotaka.meaning: a student who begged the Buddha to free him from doubt

far shore.meaning: the poems' image for freedom: the other side of the flood

flood.meaning: Pali ogha: the current of craving and suffering to be crossed

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 5.6 (Dhotakamanavapuccha, Dhotaka's question, in the Parayanavagga)

notes: Dhotaka's question paraphrased (Sn 5.6 in the common numbering). Confirm: Dhotaka first asks to hear the Buddha's voice to train for his own quenching; the Buddha: be ardent, prudent, mindful, and train; Dhotaka sees a brahmin who owns nothing, bows and asks to be released from doubts; 'I am not able to release anyone in the world who has doubt; knowing the best Dhamma, you will cross this flood'; then a peace not by hearsay, seen here; whatever is known above, below, across, in the middle, know it as a tie (sanga) in the world; don't make craving for becoming.
'Has come a long way with other students': from the Parayana prologue (Bavari's students travel to the Buddha); confirm it's fair to say for Dhotaka.
howItsDone alludes to Dhammapada 276 ('the Tathagatas only point the way'), paraphrased, not quoted.
Story shape: hook drops into the scene (the bow, the 'I can't'); the teach answers what the no means.
v3 storyline (Mai, day 8 of 14): Mai asks the art teacher, Ms. Reyes (a fictional teacher), to choose the mural design; she declines and leaves it to Mai, Ava and Jun.
